newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA accepts "painful" fallout from Basque killing.
newsitem.headline: ETA accepts "painful" fallout from Basque killing.

text.p: The Basque guerrilla group ETA declared on Wednesday it would accept the "crude and painful" consequences of its killing of a young Spanish politician earlier this month.
In its first communique since it sparked national outrage with the assassination of Miguel Angel Blanco, ETA formally claimed responsibility for the kidnap and murder.

ETA had left no doubt of its involvement in Blanco's killing. It gave the Spanish government a 48-hour deadline to meet its demands after kidnapping him on July 10, then shot him twice in the head and dumped him on a roadside.

The separatist group said in a statement published in the radical Basque newspaper Egin, its usual mouthpiece: "ETA assumes and will assume in the future, with its head held high, the consequences of the conflict as crude and painful as they may be".

"ETA assumes, through this communique, total responsibility for the arrest, and later execution after the 48-hour deadline passed, of the Popular Party member and Ermua town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco," ETA said in its statement.

ETA, which has killed around 800 people in a violent campaign for a Basque state over the past 29 years, reiterated that it was ready to lay down its arms if the government met its demands for Basque self-determination.
"The Spanish government knows for sure that ETA's hand is held out for peace," the group said. The government has refused to negotiate with ETA until it renounces violence.

Blanco's killing was a turning point for Spanish public opinion. Millions of Spaniards, incensed by the assassination of Blanco, an ordinary, low-ranking functionary, took to the streets last week to vent their anger.

Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, head of the Popular Party to which Blanco belonged, led marches in the Basque region and the capital Madrid. His party has planned a memorial service for Wednesday evening.
Three people suspected of belonging to a pro-ETA youth group were arrested on Wednesday after they attacked an employment office in the Basque regional capital Vitoria.
Faced with growing public opposition after Blanco's killing, ETA said Spain had "created collective hysteria" aimed at criminalising the Basque separatist movement.
Egin said the statement differed from previous rebel communiques in that it was addressed to Spaniards and written in Spanish rather than in the Basque language Euskera.

Wednesday's statement followed two days of protests by ETA supporters angered by the death of one of their imprisoned militants, found hanged in his cell in an apparent suicide on Sunday. They blamed the government for his death.

The Basque regional government has banned two demonstrations called by ETA's political wing, Herri Batasuna, in support of ETA. The party respected the order, calling off a march planned for last weekend, but has sought court permission to hold it this Sunday.
With anti-ETA sentiment still running high, authorities fear the demonstration could provoke street clashes.
